nameStory: This tiny plant gets its "stag's-horn" name from its branching pattern that resembles the antlers of a deer or elk. The "arctic" part of its name hints at its love of cold, northern climates where it thrives in conditions that would challenge many other plants. Like a miniature version of antlers scattered across the forest floor, these clubmosses create their own prehistoric landscape.
description: Arctic stag's-horn clubmoss is a low-growing, evergreen plant that looks like a tiny coniferous tree sprawling along the ground. It forms dense mats of branching stems covered in small, needle-like leaves that give it a soft, fuzzy appearance. This ancient plant is actually more closely related to ferns than to true mosses, and it typically grows only a few inches tall but can spread widely across suitable habitat. It's a remnant from the time when giant clubmosses dominated prehistoric forests millions of years ago.

idTips.label: Single cone feature
idTips.description: Look for just one yellowish, cylindrical cone per stem tip - this is the key difference from its cousin, regular stag's-horn clubmoss which usually has 2-4 cones branching from each stem

idTips.label: Branching pattern
idTips.description: Stems branch repeatedly in a Y-shaped pattern, creating an antler-like appearance when viewed from above, with each branch becoming progressively smaller toward the tips

idTips.label: Leaf texture
idTips.description: Tiny, scale-like leaves wrap around the stems like overlapping shingles, feeling soft and slightly fuzzy to the touch, not prickly like pine needles

idTips.label: Growth form
idTips.description: Creates low, spreading mats that hug the ground, with horizontal stems sending up vertical branches that rarely exceed 6 inches in height

idTips.label: Color and texture
idTips.description: Maintains a fresh, bright green color year-round with a velvety appearance, and the whole plant feels surprisingly sturdy despite its delicate look

habitat: In New England, arctic stag's-horn clubmoss is found in the coldest, most northern locations, particularly in high-elevation areas of Vermont, New Hampshire, and Maine. It prefers acidic, well-drained soils in coniferous forests, often growing among sphagnum moss, blueberries, and under spruce and fir trees. You're most likely to encounter it in boreal forest environments and on mountain slopes where conditions mirror its preferred arctic and subarctic climate.

seasonality.spring: New growth begins to emerge as a bright, fresh green that stands out against the darker winter foliage. This is when the plant is most actively growing and easiest to spot.
seasonality.summer: Yellowish spore cones develop at stem tips, making identification easier. The plant reaches its fullest, most robust appearance during the growing season.
seasonality.fall: Spore cones mature and release their powdery spores, sometimes creating small yellow puffs when disturbed. The evergreen foliage remains bright green.
seasonality.winter: Stays green under snow cover, making it one of the few plants providing color in the winter forest. Look for it in areas where snow has melted or blown away.

funFact: This tiny ground-hugger is actually a living fossil whose giant ancestors grew as tall as trees 300 million years ago and formed the coal deposits we use today - meaning every time you see one, you're looking at a miniature version of the plants that powered the industrial revolution!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with regular stag's-horn clubmoss (Lycopodium clavatum), but remember "one cone, arctic zone" - arctic stag's-horn almost always has just one cone per stem tip, while regular stag's-horn typically has 2-4 cones branching from each stem like a tiny candelabra.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "moss," clubmosses aren't actually mosses at all - they're more closely related to ferns and reproduce with spores rather than seeds. The spores were once collected and used as flash powder for early photography because they burn so brightly and quickly when ignited.
compareHints: Arctic stag's-horn clubmoss differs from regular stag's-horn clubmoss primarily in its cone arrangement - arctic has typically one cone per stem while regular stag's-horn has multiple cones branching from each stem tip. Arctic stag's-horn also tends to be found in colder, more northern locations and higher elevations. Both species can sometimes grow in the same area but maintain their distinct characteristics and don't interbreed.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Arctic stag's-horn clubmoss, the only other Lycopodium species in New England, is much rarer and found only in high-elevation bogs and alpine areas.
